entries.title: GDP report to give insight before Election Day. And, Israel's election is deadlocked
entries.summary: Economists expect the GDP report to show economic growth, but say that growth is "fragile." And, after 90% of the votes in Israel have been counted, no clear winner has emerged.
entries.content:
Midterm Spending Blitz, GDP & Inflations Reports, Israel Election Deadlock & Iran War

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

As Election Day approaches, data suggest that the focus is now less on whether a Democratic wave will happen and more on its potential magnitude. Democrats continue to invest in competitive Republican-dominated races, and Republicans are matching those efforts. An NPR analysis found 70 districts where both Democrats and Republicans are investing more than six figures in their final messaging. These are the races to watch.

  • 🎧 Former President Barack Obama campaigned last night in Georgia for Democrats, highlighting the high cost of living and how Trump's policies contribute to rising prices, NPR's Stephen Fowler tells Up First. Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is likely to win the Senate race, while Georgia's governor race remains uncertain. Millions have already cast their votes early, and Fowler says data show increased turnout among Latino and young voters in Democratic areas, as well as among non-supervoters, who typically don't participate in primaries. The trend creates some uncertainty around what the final electorate will look like, and indicates that Republicans will have to rely on a large Election Day turnout to stay competitive, Fowler says.
  • ➡️ A federal judge has denied the Department of Justice's emergency request to halt the processing of ballots for 20,000 individuals it identified as "likely" noncitizens. The department filed a notice that it is appealing the decision.
  • ➡️ Across the U.S., voters will see 145 statewide ballot measures on the November ballot, according to Ballotpedia. Key themes include abortion, LGBTQ+ rights, taxes, and voting.
  • ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Americans will receive a final reading on the country's gross domestic product and the state of inflation today before next week's midterm election. The report will show whether the economy grew faster in the summer compared to spring. Economists expect GDP to be higher, but some say the growth feels delicate.

  • 🎧 The tech industry's continued investment in artificial intelligence and consumer spending are driving the GDP, NPR's Stephan Bisaha says. But economist Mark Zandi tells him it's a "very, very fragile growth." Zandi blames inflation for this sense of fragility. Consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, and prices are outpacing wage growth. After keeping interest rates steady yesterday, the Fed will be paying close attention to today's inflation reading from the Commerce Department.

Israel's election is in a deadlock. More than 90% of the votes have been counted, and no candidate has a clear path to forming a coalition. Parties need 61 seats in parliament for a majority. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies have secured 53 seats, while his top rival Gadi Eisenkot and his allies have garnered 48.

  • 🎧 NPR's Daniel Estrin says there are several options for breaking the impasse. Eisenkot's camp could win by partnering with Arab-led parties, which recently secured a record 19 seats in parliament, NPR's Daniel Estrin says. But this partnership seems unlikely due to the political risks. Estrin says Arab political leaders in Israel have been demonized. Israel could hold repeat elections, but Eisenkot doesn't want that because the opposition would have a hard time getting votes a second time. Estrin says Eisenkot will be under pressure to enter a unity government with Netanyahu, especially if Israel launches a new war with Iran.

A lawsuit filed yesterday against the Department of Education alleges that the Trump administration is illegally refusing to follow the rules of a program known as "closed school discharge." For more than three decades, federal law has required the U.S. Secretary of Education to cancel debts for qualified borrowers when their schools close unexpectedly. Student Defense, a nonprofit borrower advocacy group, filed the suit on behalf of potentially thousands of borrowers. The Education Department told NPR it stands by its implementation of the program.

Today's listen

Bernie Taupin is Elton John's lyricist on nearly every album. Now, for the first time in 40 years, he's stepping into the spotlight. His new album, The Sea Has No Mercy, features a collection of songs entirely written and sung by him. Taupin admits that until recently, he hadn't considered writing for himself, but now he's ready to share his own musical voice. He tells Morning Edition's A Martínez that more so than a songwriter and a lyricist, Taupin thinks of himself as a storyteller. Listen to snippets of the album and hear about how Taupin has been able to keep his and John's relationship so strong.

Life advice

Medicare's open enrollment window runs through Dec. 7. More than half of Americans in Medicare choose a Medicare Advantage plan, which is run by private insurers instead of the federal government. Medicare Advantage is popular because it covers dental and vision, often with lower premiums than traditional Medicare. But private carriers can pick and choose where it's offered, and withdraw from unprofitable communities. Over the last three years, insurers have left regions on an increasingly large scale, according to recent JAMA research. Here are some tips to help navigate Medicare open enrollment this year:

  • ➡️ Check if your Medicare Advantage plan is still offered. Plans closing should have sent letters in early October. You can also log in to Medicare.gov to verify your plan's status.
  • ➡️ Try calling your state's State Health Insurance Assistance Program. It's free, federally mandated and offers unbiased information on all options. Visit shiphelp.org to find your state's program.
  • ➡️ Look for local Medicare counseling services. Brokers can be helpful, but make sure to choose one who discusses all your options, including traditional Medicare and supplemental plans.
  • ➡️ Double-check anything you see on Medicare's Plan Finder with your doctor's office or other Medicare assister.
  • ➡️ Be cautious about sharing your personal information, such as your phone number. Some online agencies may sell it, leading to spam calls and potential scams.

3 things to know before you go

  • American automakers reported increased revenues for the third quarter but face serious challenges. They are paying more for key components like computer chips, steel and copper, as well as higher transport fuel costs.
  • A hacking group breached the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's personnel files yesterday, exposing the names, phone numbers and addresses of over 40,000 DHS agents and associates, including those in undercover operations.
  • The Department of Health and Human Services announced a new policy that will let small compounding pharmacies make six peptides that haven't been approved by the Food and Drug Administration.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

entries.title: How AI drones are influencing the course of the Ukraine war
entries.summary: Artificial intelligence is making drones faster and more capable. Russia and Ukraine both use AI-powered drones, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that AI could lead decisions on the battlefield as soon as next year.
entries.content:
KYIV, Ukraine — Like many tech entrepreneurs in Ukraine, Yaroslav Azhnyuk turned to developing drone warfare after Russia's 2022 invasion.

Drones have transformed the way wars are fought. Azhnyuk says artificial intelligence is making drones faster and more capable.

"When the other side has orders of magnitudes higher capabilities, it gives you an asymmetric advantage," he says. "It can make you 10,000 times more effective."

Azhnyuk runs the Ukraine-based defense firms The Fourth Law and Odd Systems. They are among the top companies producing AI-powered drones in Ukraine. Dozens of Ukrainian military units already use their autonomous drone, called the Lupynis-10-TFL-1.

Russia is also deploying AI-enabled drones against Ukraine. AI warfare is part of a high-tech arms race that has many worried, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He has warned that AI could lead decisions on the battlefield as soon as next year.

Azhnyuk told NPR that he acknowledges the concern over destructive weapons but says it's not specific to AI.

"It has been with humanity since the invention of fire or steel," he says. "Any kind of tool can be used for good or for bad. And in the end, it's the human that decides how to use that tool."

Cameras that "fling explosives"

Azhnyuk is 37, a gregarious computer scientist who hails from a family of scholars and scientists. NPR meets him in a conference room in Kyiv; for security reasons he asked us not to reveal much else about the location.

He worked for years in Silicon Valley and started several companies, including Petcube, which makes smartphone-powered cameras that use artificial intelligence to watch and even entertain pets while they're alone.

"These cameras allow pet parents to watch pets when they're not at home," he says, "and fling treats to them and shine a laser toy for them. We sold a million of these devices that are quite popular in the U.S."

After Russia launched its full-scale war, Azhnyuk, by then living in Ukraine, pivoted to the defense space.

"I was like, OK, I've got to move on from Petcube and do something to protect my country," he says. "And so now we're making not cameras that fling treats but cameras that fling explosives at people who came to occupy our land."

The cameras he's talking about are part of an image recognition system incorporated into first-person-view or FPV drones.

"We are leaders in autonomous drones and thermal cameras," he says.

A drone named after a poet

The autonomous Lupynis TFL-1 drone combines a small, affordable FPV drone with an autonomous terminal guidance unit. That means the drone has an onboard computer and AI technology that takes control during the last 500 meters (or 0.3 miles) of the flight.

"But it's very different from, say, the kind of AI that sits on those data centers that power Claude," he says. "Or even the kind of AI that does self-driving for your Tesla."

Azhnyuk says this AI technology uses simple tools to recognize images and make smart software "which then allows you either to navigate autonomously without a human or to choose a target autonomously or to fly toward the target autonomously."

The Fourth Law's autonomous drone is named after the 20th century Ukrainian poet and political activist Anatoliy Lupynis, who endured decades of Soviet imprisonment and psychiatric torture. The company named all its weapons after Ukrainian intellectuals and artists killed or persecuted by Russians in the last century.

"It is important for us to help to resurrect those people," Azhnyuk says. "Their ideas are still with us. And now they're fighting back."

"The drone is doing everything itself"

The Fourth Law teams test the Lupynis TFL-1 drones every day. We meet one team in an overgrown field outside Kyiv. They've set up a fold-out table near a copse of trees and a hornets' nest.

A slight, sandy-haired man stands up from the fold-out table and says he's the head of the test and integration team. He uses the military call sign Stab. The Fourth Law asked NPR not to reveal this location or the identities of those who work here for security reasons.

Stab points to a drone.

"So you see here is our camera, plus the microcomputer inside this 3-D model," Stab says. "All of the mind is here," he adds with a laugh.

The microcomputer inside the drone runs on a deep-learning neural network that uses hours of combat footage to recognize targets.

"Like vehicles, light-armored vehicles, tanks, and flying objects," he says.

The drone begins its flight guided by a pilot, who also asked us to use his call sign, Professor. He navigates the drone with a control stick. He selects a target and checks a video monitor. Then he sees a red flash.

"That means it has locked," Stab says.

The drone has locked onto its target: a dilapidated car an employee is driving along a dirt road. Professor lets go of the control stick. The drone flies itself to the car. The microcomputer inside constantly runs algorithms to keep it on course.

"See, Professor is doing nothing, and the drone is doing everything itself," Stab says.

On the battlefield, the drone would carry an explosive to hit the car. The test drone doesn't have one.

Stab says AI drones are useful because they're hard to jam. He also insists safeguards are in place so The Fourth Law drones won't go rogue. Humans select the target, he says.

Survival vs. the ethics of AI

Back in the conference room, Azhnyuk says his company's AI-powered drones are not killer robots.

"They're very far from a Terminator kind of scenario, right?" he says. "These are just sort of calculators. Like they're no more likely for a Terminator uprising than a warehouse with artillery shells."

He does acknowledge, though, that AI is developing quickly. "It's not unthinkable," he says, "to imagine that some years in the future there will be drones that will be able to make their own decisions on designating targets or not."

That's the future. Right now he is focused on what Ukraine needs today.

"Our adversaries are using the very same technologies, and if they use AI for decision-making in an offensive scenario, and if we refuse to use AI in decision-making in a defensive scenario, we've lost, right?" he says. "Because their systems are capable of making decisions in microseconds, and human control takes minutes, hours and sometimes days."

If Ukraine loses, he says, "there's no way for us to argue about the ethics of AI."

The most important thing, he says, is don't die.

NPR's Polina Lytvynova contributed to this story from Kyiv.

entries.title: Tariffs, diesel and computer chips are driving up costs for automakers
entries.summary: American auto companies say they are paying more for key components like computer chips, steel and copper — plus the fuel needed to transport their products.
entries.content:
Tariffs, diesel and computer chips are driving up costs for automakers

Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help.

American automakers are reporting their third quarter earnings, and they're saying revenues are up, but they're also facing some serious headwinds.

Or as Mike Wall, an analyst at the automotive data company Mobility Global, put it: If this year was a book about the auto industry, "It would be a mix of suspense and thrills and maybe a little bit of comedy and a little bit of horror."

For the thrills: Auto companies are doing well when it comes to selling big cars and light-duty trucks. General Motors reported its sales of light-duty trucks rose 9% in the past year. Ford's F-Series trucks continue to be a company bestseller. Stellantis' pickup sales in the U.S. rose 34%.

And revenues overall are up: General Motors reported its revenue was up 2.9% in the past year; for Ford it was a 2% rise and Stellantis was up 1%.

To analysts, all of this signals that consumers are still buying vehicles — despite concerns about affordability. The average new vehicle transaction price was just over $50,000 in September, close to a record high, according to the Kelley Blue Book. Broadly speaking, customers are paying more for high-end trims and for bigger vehicles, which tend to be more profitable for the auto companies.

"Customers have been resilient amid higher fuel prices, interest rates and inflation," said Sherry Ann House, Ford's chief financial officer, on a call with investors.

But now for the suspense: The Detroit Three automakers are also cautioning investors that it's getting more expensive to make cars. Key materials like steel, copper and computer chips have all gotten pricier.

"Should we see prices at this level, it makes that more challenging heading into next year," Paul Jacobson, the chief financial officer of General Motors, said on the company's earnings call.

On the call for Stellantis, which owns Chrysler and Jeep, CEO Antonio Filosa noted that higher prices for memory chips and other raw materials "will be an industry-wide phenomenon to work with."

Tariffs, fuel and rising chip prices

Since 2025, the Trump administration has put additional tariffs on imported materials like steel, aluminum and copper. Much of a car's frame — and weight — is steel. So are nuts and bolts.

Copper, critical for a car's wiring and for electric vehicle batteries, has also grown more expensive — both because of tariffs and because there's more global demand for it, especially as the need for EV batteries grows. Plus, copper wire is also in high demand for data centers.

Then there are the costs of computer memory chips, which are used in a car's electronics, and are more expensive due to a tight supply chain and demand from many industries, including from AI.

Plus, there are other logistics costs. To bring vehicles from factory floors to dealerships, they get shipped on trucks, many of which run on diesel. The average price for a gallon has been hovering around $6.35, just short of its September all-time high, according to AAA. 

High diesel prices play out in other ways too. The U.S. and Canada have closely intertwined auto supply chains and parts often cross the border several times as they get shaped into a car. That movement becomes more expensive when fuel is pricier — and when the U.S. tariffs Canadian goods.

"Higher fuel prices are impacting our freight and energy costs. But notably, we are not seeing it impact customer demand for trucks and fleet vehicles at this point," said House, the CFO of Ford.

In a report to investors, General Motors forecast that the cost of materials including computer chips and diesel would run the company as much as $2 billion this year. GM is also still paying about $2.5 billion in tariff costs, Jacobson said — which was lower than the company's earlier forecasts, partially offset thanks to tariff refunds.

In Ford's earnings call, CEO Jim Farley noted a similar figure: "We currently expect commodities, memory and logistics costs to represent a year-over-year headwind of about $2 billion at Ford."

Farley and House both said growth in other parts of Ford's business, as well as software services and parts, are helping offset these costs.

On their call, Stellantis executives said they would provide more information about these costs in the fourth quarter.

All of this is disruptive for an industry that is not built for high-speed changes. It takes time and money for carmakers to plan which vehicles to build, how many, and to line up supply chains.

" This is an industry that moves at a glacial pace between generations, between vehicles, between plants," said Sam Fiorani, a vice president for Auto Forecast Solutions. "And so when you throw in tariffs and you throw in all kinds of disruptions between countries, it throws off the supply chain and the calculation for profit and loss."

The electric transition

This quarter marked a full year since the demise of the $7,500 federal tax credit, which incentivized car buyers to purchase electric vehicles. Congress nixed it as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and the credit ended on Sept. 30, 2025.

Data from the car analytics platforms Edmunds and Cox Automotive shows that after the credit went away, EV sales dropped nationally.

Tesla, which only makes EVs, reported that their global sales fell during the quarter, compared with the same period last year.

General Motors reported that its third quarter sales were down 6% overall compared to the previous year, partly because of the "smaller EV market."

On GM's call, Jacobson singled out the end of the tax credit as a reason for lower EV sales. He said the company plans to keep making electric vehicles, and that it's "right-sizing" its capacity and aligning its production with demand. "We think with these oil prices and these fuel prices that EV penetration may continue to go up, and we want to make sure we're ready for that," he said.

On Ford's call, executives didn't address EV sales, but they were enthusiastic about the Fathom, an electric truck the company plans to make available as a pre-order in early 2027, priced under $30,000.

But there are two bright spots for automakers when it comes to EVs. First, after last autumn's drop, EV sales have leveled out. As of September, they now make up about 6% of new car sales in the U.S., according to Edmunds.

American shoppers have also taken a greater interest in hybrids, especially given high fuel prices. Sales of hybrids are up 27% in the past year, according to Edmunds.

American automakers have noticed this trend, said Wall. "We have seen more inclination and more movement towards hybrids, and some automakers are adjusting their product plans accordingly," he said. But he added, gas-powered cars are still driving the profits of the big companies.

When it comes to electric vehicles, the companies are stuck in a kind of Catch-22. On the one hand, they're international companies — and EV demand is growing globally. Over 30 percent of new cars sold in Europe last year were electric. In China, more than half were, according to the International Energy Agency.

But EV demand in the U.S. just isn't the same. American drivers have long expressed concerns about limited range, charging infrastructure, or the cost of replacing an enormous lithium-ion battery.

"The thinking 10 years ago was we're going to skip hybrids and go right to electric vehicles. So we saw a lot of investment in factories, in battery plants, in new platforms to build fully electric vehicles," Fiorani said. But "when that volume didn't show up, they had to backtrack and develop new internal combustion vehicles going forward."

Fiorani expects to see the Detroit Three automakers offer more hybrid vehicles in the coming years, he said, "because this transition towards fully electric vehicles is going to take a lot longer than they anticipated."

Tesla's regaining ground

The Detroit Three's pullback in electric vehicles has given Tesla a leading edge — again. The company's third quarter revenue is about the same as it was this time last year, but its market share has grown.

Tesla used to sell the majority of EVs in the U.S. In 2024 and 2025, Tesla lost that lead. This year, it's winning the majority back: almost 52% of new EV sales in the U.S. have been Teslas, according to Edmunds.

"It makes sense that Tesla is clawing back market share," Ivan Drury, the director of industry insights at Edmunds, wrote in an email to NPR. Between other automakers peeling back some of their investments, plus the cancellation of the credit, Drury said, many buyers are probably going with what they know.

"Tesla is like the Kleenex of EVs," he continued. "Many people just default to them regardless of other offerings."

Still, on Tesla's earnings call, CEO Elon Musk did not spend much time talking about cars. He said they're focused on building new technologies, like robotaxis and humanoid robots, and they're investing a ton in these endeavors. Their capital expenditures this year are almost double from this time last year.

And on an earnings call for his rocket company SpaceX, Musk hinted at the possibility of a merger between the two companies, saying that special committees at each were discussing it. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," he told investors. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders would have to be supportive of this."

While analysts say there is some technological overlap between the two companies, a merger could be a hard sell for some Tesla shareholders, who would need to embrace adding SpaceX's business portfolio — Starlink satellites, the Grok AI chatbot, the X.com social media site — to Tesla's automotive business.

entries.title: These are the House races to watch in the 2026 midterm election on Nov. 3
entries.summary: An NPR analysis finds 70 House districts where Democrats and Republicans are each investing more than six figures in advertising during the final few days of the election, including in deep red areas.
entries.content:
These are the House races to watch in the 2026 midterm election on Nov. 3

In the final week of the 2026 midterm election, ad spending data suggests the core battle is less about stopping a Democratic wave in the House, and more about figuring out how high it crests.

An NPR analysis finds the final competitive House landscape is expansive, including 70 districts where both parties are investing at least six figures per district into their final days of messaging.

Loading...

That includes more than $10 million each in toss up districts in Michigan, North Carolina, New York and Florida; seven figure ad buys in deep-red communities across Tennessee, Oklahoma and Arkansas and last-minute resources to districts where gerrymandering by Republicans could backfire.

In a midterm environment that disfavors the party in power, Republicans' narrow 218-214 seat advantage in the House appears all but certain to give way to Democratic control. The latest ratings from the Cook Political Report finds Democrats favored in 220 seats, 17 listed as "toss-ups" and another 30 that are potentially competitive but lean toward the GOP.

Loading...

Competitive races on paper

Most of the seats that saw narrow margins in the 2024 presidential election cycle have shifted the way of the Democrats, especially in the 10 districts that voted for one party's presidential candidate and the other party's House nominee.

That includes seats held by Democratic Reps. Adam Gray (CA-13), Nellie Pou (NJ-09) and Marie Gluesenkamp-Perez (WA-03) and retiring Republican Rep. Don Bacon (NE-02).

All four of those districts have seen Republicans slash ad reservations in recent weeks, according to AdImpact data.

The latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll finds Democrats have a 10-point advantage among registered voters and 8 points with likely voters on the generic congressional ballot. That means a far broader number of seats are competitive on paper, before accounting for candidate quality or outside spending.

Cost of living remains the top concern for voters, as rising gas prices, tariffs and the ongoing war in Iran factor into economic woes for many Americans. At the same time, a record number of Congressional retirement announcements has been amplified by an anti-incumbency streak in primary elections.

A wave of mid-decade redistricting after a Supreme Court decision that further rolled back part of the Voting Rights Act further scrambled the map, as Republicans shifted boundary lines to add more conservative voters into districts held by Democratic Reps. Marcy Kaptur (OH-09), Don Davis (NC-01), Shomari Figures (AL-02) and Darren Soto (FL-09).

(Democrats did the same in California for the districts currently held by Republican Reps. James Gallagher (CA-01), David Valadao (CA-22), Ken Calvert (CA-41), Darrell Issa (CA-48) and independent Kevin Kiley (CA-06)).

Only Figures and Soto are in districts that are rated as currently favoring Republicans.

Big spending in many places

Loading...

As millions of voters have already cast their ballots in the midterms, there are dozens of races Democrats and Republicans consider worthy of heavy investment in the final hours to help shape the outcome.

Most expensive among them: Michigan's 7th District and North Carolina's 1st District —each with more than $12 million in spending planned; Florida's 14th, 22nd and 25th Districts; New York's 17th District; Iowa's 2nd and 3rd Districts and a slew of other races that either favor Democrats or are considered toss ups.

They include seats redrawn by Republicans this year to minimize Democratic voting power, like Alabama's 2nd District and Tennessee's 9th District and districts where voters backed Trump in 2024 by more than 10 points like Kentucky's 6th District and Arkansas' 2nd District.

In all, the 70 races that have at least six figures of ad spending from each party voted for Trump by an average of 9 points in 2024.

There are 60 districts that are listed as priorities of both the Democratic and Republican House campaign arms, highlighting the impact of the Trump administration's unpopularity with voters over the last year.

Not every race will end up close or see party control change hands. Many of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee's "Districts In Play," for example, gave Trump closer to 60% of the vote in 2024 and have seen little-to-no ad spend from either party.

entries.title: State ballots let voters decide on abortion, taxes, transgender restrictions
entries.summary: Missouri voters could ban abortion - after they just removed a ban two years ago. California voters could tax billionaires 5% of their wealth.
entries.content:
State ballots let voters decide on abortion, taxes, transgender restrictions

Whether or not they live in a competitive congressional district, voters in many states will be deciding on statewide ballot measures with a chance to make law themselves.

There are 145 statewide ballot measures on the November ballot, according to Ballotpedia, which tracks elections.

In some cases the questions were put on the ballot with petition drives by citizens frustrated with the actions - or lack of action - by their state lawmakers. In many cases, legislatures go to the voters with amendments to their state constitution.

There are common themes across the country: many of the most high profile referenda are on abortion, LGBTQ+ rights, taxes, and voting.

Four years after Dobbs, states are still going back and forth on abortion

Four states have abortion on the ballot. That comes after a flurry of ballot measures on the issue since federal protections for the procedure from Roe v. Wade were overturned by the Dobbs decision in 2022.

Just two years ago, Missouri voters nullified what had been one of the strictest abortion bans in the country. But the Republican-led legislature has put the question back on the ballot. And lawmakers crafted a single question that includes both a near-total ban on abortion and prohibitions on gender-affirming medical treatments for minors.

Much of the advertising for the measure just mentions the gender-affirming care ban, which would go into the state constitution to strengthen bans already in state law.

Abortion is legal in Nevada and Virginia but voters in both states will have a chance to put those rights in the state constitution. That would make it harder for future legislatures to ban abortion.

A vote in Idaho could overturn that state's near-total ban on abortion.

States consider transgender restrictions or guaranteeing LGBTQ+ rights

Rights for LGBTQ+ people have been hotly contested in the states in recent years. Several states have them on the ballot.

In Vermont a proposal would amend the state constitution to include an equal protection clause that would guarantee rights for gender identity and gender expression.

Virginia voters could strengthen laws allowing same-sex marriage. The state currently has an old ban on same-sex marriage in its constitution - although it is not in force due to a 2015 US Supreme Court decision. Voters are deciding whether to replace that language through an amendment that would define marriage as between any two adults regardless of race, sex, or gender.

Arizona and Colorado have proposals to ban transgender students in girls school and college sports, with Arizona expanding a current ban by including restrictions on locker rooms and other areas.

A proposal in Washington state would require that a student wanting to play girls sports have their biological sex confirmed by their healthcare provider based on, "the student's reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels."

A billionaire tax highlights fiscal measures

Taxes and state finances make up the largest category of ballot measures.

The highest-profile proposition is in California, where voters could impose a novel kind of billionaire tax. Prop. 40 asks voters to approve a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires, including their ownership in companies.

Proponents say the Republican Congress gave tax breaks to billionaires by cutting health care programs so it's fair to tax them to make up the cuts. Opponents, including some prominent Democrats, say it will just chase billionaires to other states. Two competing measures on the same ballot would block the tax.

A coalition of progressive Coloradans is backing a proposal that could result in higher income taxes for those making over $500,000 a year.

States are also putting limits on taxation before voters: Tennessee's legislature sent voters a proposal to ban state-mandated property taxes. Iowa's General Assembly is asking voters to approve a constitutional amendment requiring certain tax law changes to go to require two-thirds of both of the legislature's chambers to pass.

Florida lawmakers put a question on the ballot that would exempt the first $150,000 of a home's value from property taxes, having huge implications for the local governments that depend on that funding.

Many states are voting about voting

In some states, voters are facing questions that could make it harder for them to change the law through their votes in the future.

Proposals in North Dakota and South Dakota would require future amendments to the state constitution to have 60% voter approval instead of a simple majority. Utah has a similar question for tax proposals.

In Missouri, voters could go the other way – making it harder for lawmakers to overturn future voter initiatives. And they face another question about whether to allow congressional redistricting that could help Republicans flip a House seat held by a Democrat in 2028.

In Maryland, voters can approve a congressional redistricting that would likely favor Democrats.

There are several other voting issues on ballots in other states.

Coloradans are considering a proposal to require ballot questions to be written in plain, 8th grade level English.

Montanans could approve a state-level work around of the Citizens United Supreme Court decision that has led to an explosion of hard-to-track money in campaigns. The measure would do that by redefining corporations so they can't give unlimited political donations. But that could be blocked by the courts.

Several states, including California, Nevada and North Carolina have proposals to require photo ID when voting.

And in Virginia, voters will decide if some people are entitled to the right to vote at all: people convicted of felonies need to have their rights restored by the governor.

Jahd Khalil covers Virginia State Politics for VPM.

entries.title: Business as a liberal art? Some high schools say yes
entries.summary: Learning about money is becoming a growing part of the high school curriculum.
entries.content:
Business as a liberal art? Some high schools say yes

AP Business lessons are helping high school students learn how to manage money

Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help

Sitting in a semicircle around their teacher, Gerri Kimble, students at Hoover High School near Birmingham, Alabama ponder a high schooler dilemma: What to do with their part-time job paychecks. These teens say they're buying loaded teas, filling the gas tank — and investing.

"I put it in index funds, like S&P and then QQQ and VOO," says junior Darshan Parmar. Kimble asks if his parents do the actual investing. Parmar says he does it himself.

One student puts 70 percent in his Roth IRA. Another contributes to a 401(k). A third says he invests directly in stocks.

"Oh you watch the markets?" Kimble asks. "Love it."

These students are among the first in the country to take a newly created Advanced Placement Business with Personal Finance course. The class is offered for the first time this year at more than 1,500 high schools across the country.

AP courses are college level classes offered in high school. Enrolled students can take an exam in order to earn college credit. Typically, these credits are for canonical subjects like English, history and chemistry.

Students at Hoover High School's AP business class however get lessons on management and finances. They learn about the outside factors that can make or break a business – political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal.

"It's a foundational piece of business that we're learning," says senior Bramley Williams.

Business is the new liberal arts

"Business is the constant learning of adaptation," says David Coleman, CEO of the College Board, the organization that creates and develops advanced placement courses for public and private schools across the country. The group also manages and administers the SAT. It created this business course because students said in AP surveys that they want to turn their ideas into jobs.

The class is designed to appeal to students who might be drawn to a more practical curriculum than a more theoretical subject such as AP economics, which was already and still is offered at high schools like this one.

Yet Coleman still considers business a new part of the liberal arts, arguing it's as important for preparing students for the world as core areas of study like math and history. Coleman says this kind of pedagogy that mixes the practical with the theoretical "could not be more useful today."

High schools are increasingly including lessons on finance

The AP course is part of a trend towards more curriculum in US high schools focused on money and finance. Thirty nine states this year require a personal finance class to graduate – four more than two years ago according to the Council for Economic Education.

Hoover High School, located in an affluent Birmingham suburb, often feels more like a college. The campus has wide open green spaces and a massive student body a bit short of 3,000, making it the largest high school in Alabama.

Many students in this class have college aspirations.

Students say the AP class is more challenging, and could improve their grade point averages (AP classes are often weighted higher than other courses).

"This AP course is a way for me to boost my GPA and learn more about a topic that I love," sophomore Damola Kukoyi at Hoover High says.

Beyond this AP business class, Hoover offers a four-year business academy with classes such as accounting and entrepreneurship.

A Federal Reserve paper from a few years ago found families in states requiring financial ed made better financial decisions. They were more likely to use stimulus checks during the COVID-19 pandemic to pay down credit card balances and refinance their mortgages while rates were low.

"When we educate youth about how to use money responsibly they're really good at doing so," says Jennifer Steele, a professor of education at American University.

Hoover High Senior Rachel Deschaine, who's enrolled in the AP business course, says general business knowledge is important too because it teaches students people and companies interact financially with the world. Her dad owned a trucking company while her brother is majoring in economics. Deschaine sees the lessons in her class in the conversation at the dinner table.

"There's a business in literally everything," she says. "If you're willing to understand how it works, it really opens up the opportunities to a person."

entries.title: Ahead of midterms, Missourians defend transgender healthcare
entries.summary: The campaign to defend access to transgender healthcare for young people in Missouri is taking an unhurried approach to talking with voters about the proposed ban.
entries.content:
Ahead of midterms, Missourians defend transgender healthcare

CREVE COEUR, Mo. — Reneé Luckfield tries not to knock like a cop.

In fact, the 29-year-old spends a lot of time thinking about how to make strangers comfortable when she shows up at their door to talk about transgender healthcare. A syncopated "tap — tap-tap-tap" sounds friendly even when she knocks loudly. In each encounter, she masks her own unease.

"Honestly, it's not something that I'm entirely comfortable with," Luckfield, a transgender woman, said while walking door to door in this affluent St. Louis suburb. "And it's not fair that we have to do this work."

Transgender issues have become a major theme in this year's midterm elections, especially in Missouri, where voters are weighing a proposed constitutional amendment to bar minors from gender-transition surgery, cross-sex hormone therapy and puberty blockers. The potential ban is part of a proposed amendment to reinstate a near-total ban on abortion in the state.

Voters in four other states will also decide on transgender issues this year: a proposed ban on transgender health care for minors in Colorado, and proposed restrictions on transgender athletes in youth sports in Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington.

Luckfield is part of an effort by the LGBTQ+ advocacy organization PROMO Missouri to defeat the Missouri measure by knocking on 100,000 doors across five of the state's largest metro areas before the election — an ambitious target the group is trying to reach with a mixture of full-time canvassers like Luckfield, the St. Louis lead, and volunteers who show up on weekends. About one out of every 10 knocks turns into a conversation, and they're aiming to have 10,000 conversations before Election Day. The group celebrated reaching 6,000 in early October, but the process is slow going, intentionally, as canvassers aim for open-ended, "transformative" conversations with potential voters.

The technique, "deep canvassing," has a history of changing people's perspectives on difficult political topics, including a 2012 campaign that overturned a gay marriage ban in Maine and a 2021 campaign for police reform in Minnesota that, while defeated, triggered new debate. Now, organizers in Missouri hope it can help stave off the latest effort in the state to permanently ban gender-affirming care for minors.

In 2023, Missouri's Republican-dominated legislature permanently blocked minors' access to gender-affirming surgeries and temporarily blocked their access to new prescriptions for puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for four years. The state is one of 27 that enacted restrictions on gender-affirming care for minors in the past five years.

The deep canvass in Missouri began in 2024, as transgender healthcare was becoming a focal point of state and national elections. President Donald Trump's campaign, and pro-Trump groups, spent millions of dollars that year attacking Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris over transgender issues, such as one declaring, "Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you."

And in Missouri that year, an amendment to add abortion protections to the state's constitution passed by fewer than 100,000 votes. Opponents argued the measure would also enable the state's ban on gender-affirming care for minors to be overturned. "NO TAX PAID CHILD SEX CHANGE SURGERY" read a sign opposing the amendment.

This year's amendment to reinstate the state's abortion ban and codify the ban on trans healthcare for minors is polling neck and neck, with 43% supportive of the bans, 44% opposed, and 13% undecided, against a margin of error of 4.09%. This most recent poll doesn't ask separately about abortion and gender-affirming care, but polling from February showed stronger support for abortion access. The deep canvassers are trying to reach voters who are against banning abortion but are more ambivalent on trans issues. That means not spending too much time talking to people who are already very opposed or very supportive of the proposed bans.

To discern people's views, canvassers are trained to ask the person they're speaking with to place themselves on a scale from 0 to 10, with 0 being totally opposed to banning abortion and 10 being totally in favor of it. Then they ask the person to use the same scale to rate their feeling toward banning "gender-transition procedures for trans minors" — language similar to what voters will see on the ballot. After each of those questions, canvassers ask why the number the person chose is right for them.

On an overcast Saturday morning in late September, with Missouri's summer heat seemingly broken at last, the sounds of lawnmowers and leaf blowers filled the air as Luckfield began knocking doors in a neighborhood 20 miles west of the Gateway Arch.

The first person who opened their door was a 10/10 in canvasser shorthand — in favor of banning abortion because of her Christian faith and in favor of banning gender-transition procedures for minors because she doesn't think children are equipped to make those decisions and doesn't think parents should either.

"I hear you," Luckfield replied. "That's everything I need from you today. Thank you very much for your time."

The exchange wasn't unusual, Luckfield said. Neither was a conversation she had later that morning with Carol Parsons, who said she was opposed to banning both abortion and gender-transition procedures for minors — a 0/0. Luckfield acknowledged Parsons' support and asked if she had any questions about the process kids go through to get care.

"I do feel that they need to be old enough to realize that that is life-changing," Parsons said. Surgery is the thing she's not sure about, she said.

"It is tricky, and it is scary to think of that happening for young kids," Luckfield acknowledged. "The phrase 'transgender procedures' — that's, I think, very deliberately chosen language to stoke that fear of surgeries in particular."

Gender-affirming surgeries for minors are rare. One study of 2019 insurance claims for nearly 23 million children found surgeries were performed at a rate of 2.1 per 100,000 for those ages 15-17, 0.1 for those 13-14, and none for those 12 and younger. Prescription treatments are also uncommon, given to fewer than 1 in 1,000 adolescents who have commercial insurance, according to another study.

Luckfield explained to Parsons that in addition to banning surgeries and hormone treatments, Missouri's proposed amendment would ban puberty blockers. She said that puberty blockers are reversible and can be prescribed at an appropriate age alongside counseling and social transitioning to give a child time to mature and make an informed decision about further transitions.

"Well, I definitely agree with that," Parsons replied. "I think that would be a good solution."

The final door Luckfield knocked on belonged to Louis Meyer, who had previously spoken to a different deep canvasser and expressed some ambivalence about transgender care for minors. This time, he told Luckfield he was fully against both bans — a 0/0. Luckfield asked what had changed his mind.

"The original question was about where my morals sit and what I would do, which is a different statement than what I want the government to dictate," Meyer replied.

Luckfield knocked on 12 doors in an hour and a half and had conversations with five people, four of whom opposed both bans. Those numbers weren't surprising, Luckfield said, in part because St. Louis County tends to be more liberal than Missouri overall. But she thinks it also reflects something larger.

She pointed to research from the Transgender Law Center finding that when people are asked about their opinions on trans issues, they tend to answer favorably, but when they are asked how they think their neighbors feel, their answers are less certain.

"People are more accepting than they think the people around them are," Luckfield said.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

entries.title: Their colleges closed, but the government refuses to erase their debts, lawsuit says
entries.summary: Federal law requires the Education Department to erase the student loans of borrowers whose colleges close suddenly. A new lawsuit claims the department isn't fully following those rules.
entries.content:
Their colleges closed, but the government refuses to erase their debts, lawsuit says

Kendrick Gaussoin remembers it all so clearly — the August day a decade ago when his dream of becoming a professional photographer suddenly collapsed.

He was driving to the Ventura, Calif., campus of Brooks Institute, the private, for-profit college where he'd been working on a bachelor's degree in photography. When he pulled up, he was surprised to find classmates and friends milling outside. The school's doors were chained.

"It was very eerie," he remembers. "Everyone was crying. Everyone felt like they'd lost everything."

Brooks had suddenly been shut down by its parent company, leaving Gaussoin and some of his classmates with enormous student loan debts and no clear path to a degree.

"I was completely discouraged," Gaussoin remembers. "I basically gave up, and I've spent the past nine years really just trying my best to move forward."

Today, though, Gaussoin is revisiting what happened to him at Brooks — and is trying to get his student loans erased.

For more than three decades, federal law has required the U.S. secretary of education to cancel the debts of qualified borrowers whose schools close suddenly, a process known as "closed school discharge." But a lawsuit filed Wednesday against the Department of Education claims the Trump administration is illegally refusing to fully follow all of the program's rules.

The lawsuit was filed in federal court by Student Defense, a nonprofit borrower advocacy group, on behalf of Gaussoin and potentially thousands of other borrowers.

The Education Department told NPR it stands by its implementation of the program.

How closed school discharge works

According to a review by the nonpartisan U.S. Government Accountability Office, between 2010 and 2020, more than 1,100 colleges closed, including Brooks, leaving 246,000 borrowers eligible for a closed school discharge.

To qualify for a traditional discharge, borrowers have to either 1) have been enrolled at the time of closure or 2) have left school no more than six months before the closure.

Gaussoin's school, Brooks Institute, closed in August 2016. But in December 2015, he took an eight-month leave of absence to work as a photographer. Because the school was closing as he returned, Gaussoin's leave put him beyond the program's standard look-back window. He had been away too long to have his loans discharged.

But nearly a decade later, in 2025, Gaussoin's luck appeared to change.

In the waning days of the Biden administration, the Education Department expanded the look-back window for borrowers who had attended several closed schools, including Brooks.

Under the change, any borrower who was enrolled as of May 6, 2015, would qualify for a loan discharge and refund of any past payments. Gaussoin was suddenly eligible.

In an order dated Jan. 6, 2025, the department's then-undersecretary, James Kvaal, wrote that the administration was expanding the window of eligibility because the schools had been closed under "exceptional circumstances," justifying more leniency for borrowers.

Denials under Trump

Gaussoin learned about the Biden-era change over the summer. On Aug. 23, 2026, he applied for his closed school discharge, noting in his application that he now falls within the new, expanded look-back window. A week later, in a letter dated Aug. 31, the Trump administration denied his request for loan forgiveness.

In the denial letter, Gaussoin was told he did not meet the traditional pre-Biden eligibility requirements. NPR asked the department why it appeared to be ignoring the Biden-era eligibility expansion, and Education Department spokesperson Ellen Keast responded with this statement:

"The Biden Administration was laser-focused on implementing unlawful policies to shift student loan debt onto the back of every single hardworking American taxpayer. Literally days before leaving office, the former Biden Under Secretary used the stroke of a (digital) pen to inappropriately expand the closed-school discharge period for certain institutions targeted by the previous Administration."

Viewing this authority as "unlawful" is new for a Trump Education Department.

In November 2019, during the first Trump administration, Education Secretary Betsy DeVos used the same authority, citing "exceptional circumstances," to expand the look-back window for borrowers who had attended the troubled Art Institute of Colorado and the Illinois Institute of Art.

"Students were failed and deserve to be made whole," DeVos said at the time. "By canceling these students' loans … as well as extending the closed school discharge period, we hope that these impacted students will now have the tools and resources they need to complete their education."

"Legally, the secretary has the authority to expand the window [of eligibility]," says Bonnie Latreille, a former top official in the office of Federal Student Aid (FSA) during the Biden administration. If the Trump administration is now trying to quietly ignore or revoke that rule change, Latreille says, "then I think that raises legal flags."

Latreille worked at FSA as the Education Department was transitioning between the Biden and Trump administrations. She says a top department official instructed her to not immediately process any closed school discharges using the expanded look-back window without approval from the incoming Trump team.

NPR spoke with two other former department officials who corroborated Latreille's story but who asked that NPR not use their names because they feared professional repercussions for speaking out.

In this week's lawsuit, attorneys at Student Defense argue that the Trump administration cannot simply ignore or abandon the Biden-era changes, because those changes were made well within the bounds of the department's legal authority.

Multiple higher education attorneys not associated with the case told NPR that if the Trump administration wants to reverse those changes, it would have to do what the Biden administration did: build a reasoned, legal explanation and then share that with the public.

The department did not respond to a request to share its legal justification for ignoring the Biden-era changes.

"This is a joke, right?"

Unbeknownst to Gaussoin, Brooks had been in trouble for years. Founded in 1945, the visual arts school was once well regarded. But after its sale in 1999, enrollment began to decline as borrowers accused Brooks of high-pressure sales tactics, lying about graduation and job placement rates and misleading students about the school's high cost.

Gaussoin's mother, Christine Gaussoin, took out Parent PLUS loans to pay for her son's education. She says the school led her to believe that her loans would be enough to cover Kendrick's costs at Brooks. The plan was for him to remain debt free.

"Then I get an email from the counselor," she remembers. "It says, 'We need more money.' And I was like, 'I'm tapped out.'"

At the time, Christine says she was living on disability while recovering from a total knee replacement.

"Then Kendrick calls me and says, 'I need you to write this letter that says I'm not your dependent anymore.' I was like, 'Really?' He's like, 'Yeah. I'm going to take out federal loans so I can finish the degree.'"

Christine pauses, remembering this conversation. "What is a mom to do?"

When Kendrick called his mother to tell her the schools' doors had been chained shut, she remembers thinking, "This is a joke, right? Really, this was a joke, because he had just taken out those federal loans, and I didn't know what to tell him."

For the past 10 years, Kendrick and his mother have both felt the weight of those loans.

He is now married with two young children and works for an online retailer. He's saddled with nearly $22,000 in student loan debt, including interest, but no degree.

"I've been working hard at just trying to survive off minimum wage," Kendrick says. "It's been really tough."

Christine says she also works in retail and owes about $28,000 that she worries she may never pay off, even though her debts also, technically, qualify for discharge under the Biden-era change. Her application for a closed school discharge was denied this month.

Christine says she regrets how she and her son fell for the promises of a troubled school.

"The school promised us that this was gonna be his ticket — to make the most money he will ever be able to [as a photographer]," she remembers.

Instead, a decade later, the school and the Gaussoins' unpaid debts are still holding them back.

entries.title: Spain reckons with 2nd deadly train crash of the year ahead of national election
entries.summary: Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year, a crash in which one train struck another from behind, killing 68 people, has raised fresh concerns about the safety of the country's rail network.
entries.content:
Spain reckons with 2nd deadly train crash of the year ahead of national election

URDA, Spain — Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year, a crash in which one train struck another from behind, killing 68 people, has raised fresh concerns about the safety of the country's rail network.

Spain's network of high-speed rail has been considered one of the nation's crowning achievements. It ranks second to China in track mileage in the world. Until this year, it had not endured a deadly crash since coming into service over three decades ago.

The collision Wednesday that turned a sleepy stretch of rail lined by olive groves into a scene of carnage came just four weeks before the country votes in a national election.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited the crash site in the central province of Toledo after regional authorities confirmed that more than 60 people had died and dozens more were being treated at hospitals.

Only in January, 46 people had died when one train jumped the track and slammed into the side of another going the opposite way in southern Spain.

Sánchez pledged an investigation into the latest collision and improvements to prevent another tragedy like the two that have shaken trust in a rail system that carried 45 million travelers last year, including millions of tourists.

"It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail," Sánchez said. "It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year."

Sánchez's government declared three days of mourning starting Thursday.

Both deadly crashes this year involved a train operated by the state-owned RENFE company and one from the privately owned IRYO. Spain only liberalized its high-speed rail service in 2021, with the Italian IRYO starting service the following year.

Political implications for Sánchez ahead of election

Sánchez has weathered many crises since taking power in 2018, staying in power and winning reelection after the COVID-19 pandemic and the global rise in inflation.

But polls show he faces another uphill battle when voters cast ballots in Spain's first national election since 2023. The new rail disaster can't help the prospects of his Socialist party.

Sánchez and other progressive parties had hoped to leverage a wave of discontent over housing costs and high rents when he called for early elections earlier this month.

About an hour before news of Wednesday's crash spread, Sánchez had posted on X a message that "There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about this country."

Now it appears he will have to handle concerns over the state of Spain's rail service along with attacks from right-wing parties over his liberal migration policies and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both he and his wife deny.

His transport minister, Óscar Puente, had to handle media questions over whether he would resign following a second major train wreck under his watch. His response was that he was fully focused on dealing with the collision, not his future.

Sánchez's main rival, Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, demanded a full investigation of the crash. The conservative leader said that in respect for the victims his party canceled its campaign events for the day.

"This is the moment to respect the dead, the injured and their families," Núñez Feijóo said. "That does not mean we will ignore the fact that Spaniards are asking tough questions that demand answers."

The far-right Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, who is likely hoping to enter a coalition government with the conservatives, did not show the same restraint.

"More dead. Another tragedy. More rage over being left to fend for ourselves, the despair and the betrayal that Spaniards are enduring," Abascal said just hours after the crash.

"I promise to work tirelessly until this government, which is a criminal organization, is sitting in a courtroom to answer for its crimes," he said.

Human error was behind the crash

Puente said that the crash was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.

Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. At that point the IRYO train was stopped near the town of Urda, while the RENFE train was 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) behind it.

But a few minutes later the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stationary IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.

Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.

Workers started to use cranes to move parts of the damaged trains late on Wednesday after a hectic day involving hundreds of emergency workers, firefighters, police and soldiers all pitching in to rescue survivors and recover bodies.
